645.title: Ardas close
645.hook: the history and hope of a whole people in one prayer
645.howItsDone: Sikhs say the full Ardas standing at the close of services and many daily prayers: it remembers the Gurus, the martyrs and the gurdwaras, makes the day's petition, and ends with good for all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, benti, and your line: your own words. Did you read your three lines again before sleep? Today we close this part of the path: the Ardas, line by line, seen whole. Day six hundred forty-five.

For thirty-five days we've taken one prayer apart, line by line, the way you might take apart a watch to see how it ticks. Now put it back together. Picture it all at once: a few minutes long, said standing, every day, in every gurdwara, in kitchens and hospital rooms and airports. And inside those few minutes, an entire people's story, from its first Guru to this morning's family asking for help with a new job.
screen: `THIRTY-FIVE DAYS, ONE PRAYER.` → `PUT IT BACK TOGETHER.` → `A WHOLE PEOPLE'S STORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole Ardas, as a map. It opens with lines from Guru Gobind Singh: first remember the Divine, then Guru Nanak, and it walks name by name through the ten Gurus, ending with the Guru Granth Sahib. Then it remembers. The Panj Piare, the five beloved ones. The four Sahibzade, Guru Gobind Singh's sons. The martyrs, named by what they endured, and those who served in the langar and kept faith under pressure. Then it turns to places: the five takhts, the seats of authority, and all the gurdwaras, including the ones left behind across the border. Then it asks. The gift of Sikhi, faith, discernment, the Name. Honor for the humble, strength for the weak, shelter for the shelterless. Then the petition, today's reason, in plain words. Forgiveness for any slip. And the last line: rising spirits, good for all. Look at the order: remember, then ask, then widen. A Sikh standing for the Ardas first places themselves inside a long line of people: Gurus, martyrs, ordinary servers. Only then do they bring their own small need. And they end by asking good for everyone. That's how one prayer can hold the history and hope of a whole people. The history is the remembering. The hope is the last line. The words have grown over time; the Rehat Maryada gives the standard text, and the remembrance of martyrs reaches into the eighteenth century and beyond. That's part of the point. The Ardas is a living prayer that a people keeps adding its story to.
screen: `FIRST REMEMBER: THE TEN GURUS.` · `THE MARTYRS AND THE PLACES.` · `THEN ASK: FOR SIKHI, FOR TODAY.` · `END WIDE: GOOD FOR ALL.` · then, large: `A WHOLE PEOPLE PRAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Walk the map in your mind, one breath for each stop. The Gurus. The five beloved ones. The martyrs. The gurdwaras, near and far. The humble and the weak. Your own reason today. Forgiveness for your slips. Good for all. Go slowly. Let each stop be a picture, not a word. If you pray, sometime today you can pray the Ardas once whole, or listen to it said in a gurdwara or a recording. If not, simply let the map rest in you. The bell holds the time.
Sahibzade, Guru Gobind Singh's sons: remembered in the Ardas alongside the Panj Piare and the martyrs, before it asks for the Name and for today, and ends with good for all.

Your line: a whole people prays. Today, think of one person who came before you and made your life possible, and say their name aloud. Tomorrow the path turns to hymns for every part of a life. Day six hundred forty-five.

646.title: A shabad for every moment
646.hook: Sikhs mark birth, marriage and death with particular hymns
646.howItsDone: Sikhs sing shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib in kirtan, and mark life's turning points with particular hymns: shabads of thanks at a birth, the lavan at a wedding, Kirtan Sohila at night and at a funeral.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sahibzade, and your line: a whole people prays. Whose name did you say aloud? Today a new part of the path begins: hymns for a whole life. Day six hundred forty-six.

Hum the first song you danced to at a wedding. Now the song that was playing in the car the summer you were seventeen. Now the one they played at your grandfather's funeral. Some songs get welded to moments like that: a private soundtrack. Sikh life has a shared soundtrack like that. The same hymns, sung at the same turning points, by family after family, generation after generation. A child born, a couple married, a life ended: each has its hymns, and some children can hum them before they can read.
screen: `THE SONG FROM THE WEDDING.` → `A PRIVATE SOUNDTRACK.` → `A SHARED ONE, FOR GENERATIONS.`

segments.voice: The word is shabad. It means word, and in Sikh usage it means two things at once. A shabad is a hymn, one composition from the Guru Granth Sahib. And the Shabad is the Word itself, the voice of the Guru, the presence of the One in sound. When a shabad is sung, Sikhs understand both are happening. And the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib are meant to be sung. The scripture is arranged by raag, musical mode, each raag with its own mood and, tradition says, its own time of day. Kirtan, singing those hymns with music, is at the heart of worship. Now look at a life. When a child is born, there are shabads of joy and thanks. When a couple marries, they walk four rounds around the Guru Granth Sahib while the lavan, four verses by Guru Ram Das, are sung. At the end of every day, and at the end of a life, Kirtan Sohila is sung. Guru Nanak even wrote a set of hymns for mourning, the alaahniaan, in Raag Vadhans, on ang 578, which turn the old songs of lament toward the One. For the next five weeks, this part of the path walks through shabads like these: hymns about wealth and greed, longing and friendship, night and morning, birth, marriage and death. Some you may recognize. Some will be new. Each one is a hymn Sikhs reach for at a particular moment of life. The idea isn't to memorize a playlist. It's to have, for every moment, words and a melody that point beyond the moment itself.
screen: `SHABAD: A HYMN, AND THE WORD.` · `ARRANGED BY RAAG, TO BE SUNG.` · `BIRTH, MARRIAGE, NIGHT, DEATH.` · `FIVE WEEKS OF SHABADS FOR A LIFE.` · then, large: `A HYMN FOR EVERY MOMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of one song tied to a memory, any song, sacred or not. Let it play in your head. Notice where it takes you: a room, a face, a season. Notice whether the feeling comes back faster than a photograph would bring it. Kirtan works with that same pull of melody. Then, if you know any shabad, even just its first line or a single Waheguru sung to a tune, let it play next. If you don't, just rest in the silence after your song. The bell holds the time.
Shabad. A hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the Word itself. Sikhs sing particular shabads at birth, marriage, the close of each day and the end of a life.
Your line: a hymn for every moment. Today, notice when a song comes into your head on its own, and ask what moment it belongs to. Day six hundred forty-six.

647.title: Palaces of pearls
647.hook: if I had palaces of pearls and jewels, may I never forget You (Sri Rag M1, ang 14)
647.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its refrain, that without the Lord the soul burns and there is no other place, is often the line congregations repeat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shabad, and your line: a hymn for every moment. What song came into your head on its own? Today, the first hymn of this stretch, and it begins in a dream house. Day six hundred forty-seven.

A real estate app, late at night. Infinity pool. Floor-to-ceiling windows over the ocean. A kitchen bigger than a whole apartment, a garden, room for everyone you love. Scroll, imagine, almost smell the sea air. Guru Nanak built a dream house too, in words. Near the very start of the Guru Granth Sahib's main body, in Sri Rag, he raises a palace wall by jeweled wall. And then he asks one question about it.
screen: `A REAL ESTATE APP AT MIDNIGHT.` → `GURU NANAK BUILDS A DREAM HOUSE.` → `THEN ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The shabad is on ang 14. It begins, in effect: if I had a palace built of pearls, inlaid with jewels, its walls plastered with musk and saffron, sandalwood and aloe, a joy to come home to. Then the turn: let it not be that, seeing all this, I go astray, forget You, and Your Name no longer comes to mind. Then the refrain, the rahao, the line tradition treats as the hymn's center: without the Lord my soul burns to ashes; I asked my Guru, and I saw there is no other place. And then he does it again, three more times, each one bigger. If the floor were paved with diamonds and rubies, and a beautiful companion waited on a jeweled bed. If I became a siddha, a yogi with miraculous powers, appearing and vanishing at will. If I became a sultan, raising armies, sitting on a throne, giving orders. Each time, the same ending: let me not forget You. Notice what Guru Nanak doesn't say. He doesn't say palaces are evil, or that beauty is a trap, or that the rich are lost. Sikh teaching doesn't ask people to give up homes, families or work; the Gurus lived as householders. The danger he names is narrower and sharper: forgetting. A beautiful thing can fill the view so completely that the Giver drops out of the picture. The hymn doesn't ask for less. It asks to remember, even with more. And it was put in Sri Rag, a raag tradition associates with evening and with seriousness. A grave melody for a dream house.
screen: `A PALACE OF PEARLS AND MUSK.` · `LEST I FORGET YOU.` · `JEWELS, POWERS, A THRONE.` · `NOT RENUNCIATION: REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `MAY I NOT FORGET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Picture your dream house. Really build it: the view, the kitchen, the light in the morning, whoever you'd want there with you. Enjoy it for a few breaths. You're allowed. Then ask Guru Nanak's question: in that house, would I still remember what matters most? Would I still call my mother, still sit quietly, still notice the person who cleans the pool? Then let the house go, gently, like setting down a heavy box. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you let go. The bell holds the time.
Rahao, the refrain, the line tradition treats as a hymn's center: here, after every luxury and power Guru Nanak imagines, it asks only this, that none of it make him forget the One.
Your line: may I not forget. Today, when you see something you want, a house, a car, a phone, say the line once before you scroll on. Day six hundred forty-seven.

648.title: Greed is a dog
648.hook: greed is a dog, falsehood a scavenger, cheating is eating carrion (Sri Rag M1, ang 15)
648.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its first-person confession, these are my deeds, is sung by the whole congregation about themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rahao, and your line: may I not forget. What did you see that you wanted? Today Guru Nanak names what's doing the wanting, and gives it a very unflattering face. Day six hundred forty-eight.

There's a dog in every neighborhood that knows exactly when the trash goes out. It can be fed an hour ago and still stand at the gate, nose working, eyes on the bag. Not because it's hungry. Because it's a dog. Some of us have met a version of that dog inside: at a buffet, in a sale, scrolling past one more thing nobody needs. One page after the dream house, Guru Nanak names that dog out loud, and he doesn't soften it.
screen: `THE DOG AT THE GATE.` → `NOT HUNGRY, JUST A DOG.` → `GURU NANAK NAMES IT.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Sri Rag, on ang 15. Its first lines run, in effect: greed is a dog; falsehood is a scavenger; cheating is eating carrion. Slandering others is putting their filth in your own mouth. Anger is a fire that burns like an outcast's pyre. Then the punch: these tastes and this self-praise, these are my deeds, O Creator. The word for greed is lab, the hungry wanting that's never full. Now, two things to notice. First, the language is harsh on purpose. Guru Nanak takes the insults of his own day, the names a caste society threw at people it looked down on, and throws them instead at the vices. It's the greed that's the dog. It's the lying that's unclean. The Gurus rejected caste outright, and here the shock of those words is turned around: the real lowness, he's saying, isn't in anyone's birth. It's in what a person does. Second, and this is the surprise: the shabad is in the first person. Not you are greedy. Not they are liars. These are my deeds. The Guru speaks the confession himself, so that anyone singing it is saying it about themselves. Nobody singing this hymn gets to point at the person across the hall. The refrain then turns toward speech: speak in a way that brings honor. Those whose deeds are good are called good at the Lord's door. So the dog isn't destiny. A dog can be noticed. A dog can be trained, or at least told no. The first step is just seeing it at the gate.
screen: `LAB: GREED, NEVER FULL.` · `INSULTS TURNED ON THE VICES.` · `THESE ARE MY DEEDS.` · `SPEAK IN A WAY THAT BRINGS HONOR.` · then, large: `MIND THE DOG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: catch greed once. Sit and think back over today or yesterday. Find one moment when you wanted more than you needed: one more helping, one more purchase, one more scroll, one more bit of credit. Don't scold yourself. Just see it, the way you'd see a dog at the gate. Notice where you felt it in your body: the chest, the hands, the eyes. Then breathe, and let it sit there without obeying it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru to it, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Lab, the hungry wanting that's never full: Guru Nanak names it, lying, cheating and slander, and confesses them as his own deeds, so everyone who sings it does the same.
Your line: mind the dog. Today, catch greed once in the act: at a meal, a store, a screen. Notice it, name it, and don't feed it this time. Day six hundred forty-eight.

649.title: The river and the fish
649.hook: You are the river, all-knowing; I am a fish, how can I find Your end (Sri Rag M1, ang 25)
649.tomorrow: The four watches of the night
649.howItsDone: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its refrain, wherever I look, there You are, is often repeated by the congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lab, and your line: mind the dog. Did you catch it at the gate? Today, a gentler animal, and a tender picture from Guru Nanak. Day six hundred forty-nine.

Here's an old riddle: does a fish know it's wet? It has never been anywhere else. Water is above it, below it, inside its gills, carrying its food, holding up its weight. The one thing a fish can't do is step back and see the water. Guru Nanak, from the land of five rivers, wrote a hymn that swims close to that riddle. In it, he doesn't play the river. He plays the fish.
screen: `DOES A FISH KNOW IT'S WET?` → `IT CAN'T STEP BACK AND SEE.` → `GURU NANAK PLAYS THE FISH.`

segments.voice: The shabad is in Sri Rag, on ang 25. It begins, in effect: You are the river, all-wise, all-seeing; I am a little fish, how could I ever find Your end? The word for the fish is machhuli, a small fish, almost affectionate. Then the refrain: wherever I look, there You are; pulled out of You, I burst and die. That's the whole hymn in one picture. The fish can't measure the river. It can't get outside it to see where it starts or ends. And it doesn't need to. It just needs to stay in it. Out of the water, a fish doesn't become free. It suffocates. Then Guru Nanak adds a very honest line. I don't know the fisherman, he says, and I don't know the net. But when pain comes, then I call on You. He's admitting what a lot of people would rather not: that we often remember the river only when we're flapping on the bank. And then a correction: You are present everywhere; I thought You were far away. Whatever I do is done in Your presence. Here's the gentle thing about this hymn. Elsewhere Gurbani talks about separation from God as a kind of exile. This shabad suggests the separation is partly an illusion. The fish thinks the river is somewhere else, because it's never seen it from outside. But it has never once been outside it. For Sikhs that's what naam, remembering the Name, does: not bringing God close, but noticing how close God has been all along.
screen: `YOU ARE THE RIVER; I AM A FISH.` · `OUT OF YOU, I DIE.` · `I CALL ON YOU WHEN PAIN COMES.` · `I THOUGHT YOU WERE FAR.` · then, large: `A FISH IN THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch water flow. If you can, run a tap slowly, or pour water from one glass into another, or look at rain, a fountain, a stream. If none is near, picture one clearly. Watch how it moves without effort, how it fills whatever shape it's given. Then notice what you're surrounded by right now: air, light, the ground holding you up, all of it unasked for. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, a fish thanking the river. The bell holds the time.
Machhuli, a little fish: Guru Nanak says, You are the river, I am a machhuli; wherever I look, You are there, and out of You I die.
Your line: a fish in the river. Today, every time you drink water, remember the fish, and notice one thing holding you up that you never asked for. Day six hundred forty-nine.

screen: `DAY 649 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FOUR WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.`

650.title: The four watches of the night
650.hook: the four watches of the night as the stages of a life (Sri Rag M1, ang 74)
650.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Sri Rag pehre in kirtan, each stanza beginning with the watch of the night and addressing the listener as vanjaariaa mitraa, O merchant friend.

segments.voice: Yesterday, machhuli, and your line: a fish in the river. What held you up today that you never asked for? Today Guru Nanak lays a whole life over a single night. Day six hundred fifty.

Before clocks, a night was measured in watches. Guards on a city wall, sailors on a ship, merchants in a caravan camped by the road: the dark was split into four stretches of about three hours each, and each one had someone awake. You'd know the watch by how the night felt. The first, still warm from the day. The deep middle ones. The last, cold and gray-blue, just before dawn. Guru Nanak took those four watches and turned them into a map of a human life.
screen: `A NIGHT IN FOUR WATCHES.` → `GUARDS, SAILORS, CARAVANS.` → `A MAP OF A HUMAN LIFE.`

segments.voice: The hymn is called a pehre, from pahar, a watch. It's in Sri Rag, beginning on ang 74, and Guru Nanak addresses it to vanjaariaa mitraa: O my merchant friend. The listener is a trader on a journey, sent out with capital, expected to come back with something to show for it. In the first watch, the hymn says, by the Lord's command you came into the womb, and there you remembered the One. You came into the world naked, and naked you'll go. In the second watch you forgot. You were passed from arm to arm, adored, the hymn says, as Krishna was in Yashoda's house, and your mother said: this is my son. Childhood and youth, beloved and busy. In the third watch your mind was fixed on wealth and on your own young body, and the Name didn't come to mind. Work, money, building a life. In the fourth watch the reaper comes. Nobody knows the hour. And the merchant's accounts are read: what did you trade your life for? It's a sobering hymn, and Sikhs sing it as one. But it isn't meant to frighten. Notice who is speaking: a friend, mitraa, calling out to a traveler while there's still night left. The point of naming the watches is that a person can wake up in any of them. A child can remember. A busy parent in the third watch can stop. Someone very old, in the cold last stretch before dawn, can still turn. The question isn't how far the night has gone. It's whether you're awake for the watch you're in.
screen: `PEHRE: A HYMN OF WATCHES.` · `O MY MERCHANT FRIEND.` · `WOMB, CHILDHOOD, WEALTH, THE REAPER.` · `WAKE UP IN ANY WATCH.` · then, large: `WHICH WATCH AM I IN?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit with the four watches. The first: beginnings, the womb, the newness. The second: being carried, loved, playing. The third: building, earning, carrying others. The fourth: the late, cold watch, the time to settle accounts. Ask honestly: which watch am I in? Don't judge the answer. Then ask the friend's question: what am I trading this watch for? If you pray, you can say Waheguru once before the bell. The bell holds the time.
Pahar, a watch, a quarter of the night: Guru Nanak's map of a life in four of them, womb, childhood, the busy middle, and the last watch, sung to a merchant friend while there's still time.
Your line: which watch am I in. Today, ask it once, and ask someone older or younger which watch they think they're in. Day six hundred fifty.

651.title: The four letters, whole
651.hook: Guru Arjan's longing letters to his father, read in full (Majh M5, ang 96–97)
651.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Majh shabad 'meraa man lochai gur darsan taaee' in kirtan, and tell the story of the letters from Lahore that led to his being named the fifth Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pahar, and your line: which watch am I in. What did you answer? Today, the week closes with letters a son wrote in the long watches of missing his father. Day six hundred fifty-one.

Early in the path we met young Arjan in Lahore. His father, Guru Ram Das, had sent him there for a family wedding and told him to stay until he was called. Weeks went by. No call came. Arjan wrote home in verse. Tradition says the first two letters never reached his father: his elder brother, Prithi Chand, kept them. So Arjan numbered the third. When Guru Ram Das read a letter marked three, he asked where one and two had gone. Today we read the letters whole, all four stanzas, in order.
screen: `ARJAN, SENT TO LAHORE.` → `TWO LETTERS NEVER ARRIVE.` → `THE THIRD IS NUMBERED.`

segments.voice: They stand in Raag Majh, on angs 96 and 97, as one shabad of four stanzas. The first, in effect: my mind longs for a sight of the Guru. It cries like the chaatrik, the rainbird that tradition says drinks only falling rain. The thirst won't go, no peace comes, without seeing my beloved. And each stanza ends: I am a sacrifice, a sacrifice, to the sight of the Guru. The second: your face is beautiful, your words bring a deep, natural peace. It's been so long since this rainbird saw water. The third, the numbered one, is the sharpest. When I can't meet you for even a moment, it's the dark age for me. When will I meet you, beloved? The night won't pass; sleep won't come. Then the fourth, written after the reunion. Tradition says Guru Ram Das sent for him, and soon named him the fifth Guru. And the last stanza turns: by good fortune I've met the Guru, and found the eternal Lord within my own home. Read whole, the letters have a shape. Longing, then memory, then near despair, then arrival. They can be heard as two loves at once: a son for his father, and a soul for the One. The shabad never pulls the two apart. Now, the week. The Ardas closed, a whole people's prayer. Then shabad, a hymn for every moment. Rahao: may I not forget. Lab. Machhuli. The four watches of a life. And the four letters: longing that gets an answer.
screen: `ONE: I CRY LIKE THE RAINBIRD.` · `TWO: SO LONG SINCE I SAW WATER.` · `THREE: A MOMENT AWAY IS A DARK AGE.` · `FOUR: FOUND IN MY OWN HOME.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE LONGING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a letter to someone you miss. Bring them to mind: someone far away, someone you've drifted from, someone who has died. Begin the letter in your head, or on paper if you have it. Start the way Arjan did, with the plain truth: I miss you. Then one thing you remember about them. Then what the missing feels like, honestly. Don't worry about sending it. If you pray, you can hold them before the One with a quiet Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Darshan, sight, seeing the beloved: Guru Arjan's four stanzas in Raag Majh long for it, like the rainbird, through the third letter's dark night, to the reunion, found in his own home.
Your line: the whole longing. Today, finish the letter you started, and if the person is living and reachable, think about sending it. Day six hundred fifty-one.

fork.setup: you're Arjan in Lahore. two letters have gone unanswered. what do you do?
options: write a third and number it.
fork.reveal: the numbered third letter revealed the missing two. Guru Ram Das called him home.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sight, seeing the beloved; the letters long for the Guru's darshan.

trapdoor: what you thought: homesick letters from a young man.
what it means: one shabad in four stanzas, longing for a father and for the One, ending in reunion.

what a scholar hears: the shabad's arc, from the chaatrik's thirst to 'found within my own home', joins the succession story to a theology of the Lord found within; the letter narrative comes from Sikh tradition.
